about: The story goes back a generation, to the fathers of Hunahpu and Xbalanque, and the narrator says that only half of it will be told. Xpiyacoc and Xmucane had two sons, born in the night: Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu. Hunhunahpu and his wife Xbaquiyalo had two sons, Hunbatz and Hunchouen, who grew wise and were taught every art: the flute, song, the blowgun, writing and painting, carving, jewelry and silverwork. Vucub Hunahpu had no wife. The two brothers did nothing but play at dice and at ball every day, two against two in the ball court, and the Voc, the messenger of Huracan, came to watch them; he was never far from the earth or from Xibalba, and could be back in the sky in an instant. The mother of Hunbatz and Hunchouen died. The brothers played on the road to Xibalba, and Huncame and Vucub Came, the lords of Xibalba, heard them: the players, they said, had no respect and no fear of them, and should be summoned to play and be beaten. The part then names the lords under the two, pair by pair, each with the sickness or death that is its office: Xiquiripat and Cuchumaquic, of the blood; Ahalpuh and Ahalq'ana, of swelling, pus and the yellow sickness; Chamiabac and Chamiaholom, the staff-bearers, who waste people to the bone; Ahalmez and Ahaltocob, who meet people at their houses and strike them down; and Xic and Patan, of sudden death on the road. The lords take counsel to hunt down the two brothers, and they covet their ball-game gear. The narrator turns to the brothers' journey to Xibalba: Hunbatz and Hunchouen stay behind, and their own downfall at the hands of Hunahpu and Xbalanque is still to come.

sentences.t: Are chicut xchi ca biyh chic v bi qui cahau ri Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: This-is again-then shall we tell also its name of-their-father the Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: And now we shall tell the name of the father of Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
sentences.n: The story of the two boys begins again, a generation back, with their fathers. chicut is chic 'again' + cut 'then' written as one word, the c shared (toggle chik'ut), as in the last part. xchi ca biyh 'we shall tell': xchi- 'shall', ca- 'we', and biyh, the verb bih 'say' with its letters in another order, as in 007 and 008. v bi 'its name', written apart. qui cahau 'their father': cahau 'father' is the word paired with chuch 'mother'; qui- 'their' because the father of both boys is meant.

sentences.t: Xcacamuh chu vi, xa pu xcacamuh vbixic, vꜩihoxic puch qui ꜭaholaxic ri Hunahpu, Xbalanque;
sentences.l: We-camuh(?) over-it, only also we-camuh(?) its-being-said, its-being-told also of-their-being-begotten the Hunahpu, Xbalanque;
sentences.i: We shall cover it over; we shall keep covered the telling and the account of how Hunahpu and Xbalanque were begotten;
sentences.n: xcacamuh: x- + ca- 'we' + camuh, a verb not otherwise known; the muh 'shade' of the first part's camuhibal 'our place of shade' may be in it, which would fit Brasseur's veil (inferred). Brasseur reads x-ka gamuh (his g is ꜫ) and renders it 'we shall throw a veil of mystery over it'; 'cover over' is taken from him and is a guess. So is the tense: x- is usually the completive ('we did'), but the sentence looks ahead. In the manuscript a struck-through x stands before the first xcacamuh and is left out; that word's a is badly formed (it could be read xcoacamuh), and it is read like the second, which is clear (MS xca|camuh). The toggle respells the letters (k, not Brasseur's q'). chu vi 'over it' (MS chuvi, the chuvi 'on top of' of earlier parts). vbixic, vꜩihoxic puch 'its being said, its being told', the couplet of the first part. qui ꜭaholaxic 'their being begotten': ꜭahol 'son (of a man)' made a verb, then a passive noun with -ax- + -ic.

sentences.t: xa nicah xchi ca biyh, xa chacab v bixic qui cahau.
sentences.l: only half shall we tell, only chacab(?) its being-said of-their-father.
sentences.i: we shall tell only half of it, only a part of the telling of their father.
sentences.n: nicah 'half' (toggle nik'aj, as in the last part). chacab pairs with nicah and is read with Brasseur, who renders xa chakab 'only a part'. In 007 the same letters were chacab 'by night' (chi + aꜫab, toggle chaq'ab'), and that sense would also fit a story told under a veil ('only in the dark'). Because the word here is not certain, the toggle respells the letters (chakab') and does not restore 007's q'. v bixic 'its being said', written apart here.

sentences.t: Vae cute vꜩihoxic.
sentences.l: This then its-telling.
sentences.i: This, then, is the account.
sentences.n: A new paragraph in the manuscript, under a large V. Vae 'this' points forward, as in the first line of the book; cute is the longer form of cut 'then'. vꜩihoxic 'its being told': v- 'its' + ꜩihoh 'tell' + passive -x- + -ic.

sentences.t: Are qui bi ri Hunhunahpu, que vꜭhaxic.
sentences.l: This their name the Hunhunahpu, thus its-being-called.
sentences.i: Their name is Hunhunahpu, as they are called.
sentences.n: Hunhunahpu is hun 'one' + Hunahpu: 'One Hunahpu', a date in the day count; his brother below is Vvcub Hunahpu, 'Seven Hunahpu' (vvcub 'seven', as in Vvcub Caquix). These two are the fathers of Hunahpu and Xbalanque. (In 005 the same name was written where the actor was the boy Hunahpu.) qui bi 'their name' gives the name to more than one, and Brasseur renders 'their name, each of them, is Ahpu' (Leur nom à chacun est Ahpu). que vꜭhaxic 'thus it is said, as they are called'.

sentences.t: Are cut qui cahau ri Xpiyacoc, Xmucane chique.
sentences.l: This then their-father the Xpiyacoc, Xmucane to-them.
sentences.i: And their parents were Xpiyacoc and Xmucane.
sentences.n: qui cahau 'their father' here covers a pair, the grandfather and grandmother: Xpiyacoc and Xmucane, the old couple of the creation, are the parents of Hunhunahpu and his brother. chique 'to them' (chi + que) closes the sentence: 'their father … to them', i.e. theirs. The English says 'parents'.

sentences.t: Cumal chi acabal xe alaxic ri Hunhunahpu, Vvcub Hunahpu, cumal Xpiyacoc, Xmucane.
sentences.l: By-them in night they-were-born the Hunhunahpu, Vvcub Hunahpu, by Xpiyacoc, Xmucane.
sentences.i: By them, in the night, Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu were born: by Xpiyacoc and Xmucane.
sentences.n: cumal 'by them', the agent of a passive, frames the sentence twice, first as a pronoun, then with the names. xe alaxic 'they were born': xe- 'they' + al 'child, bear a child' + passive -ax- + -ic; al is the root of Alom 'Child-Bearer'. chi acabal 'in the night': the manuscript has chiacabal at the line end; Brasseur prints chi agab, without -al. It is printed as the image shows; toggle aq'ab'al, as in 003. Brasseur's note takes 'in the night' as before the course of their sun, that is, before their calendar and institutions, which is an interpretation. MS vvcub | hun ahpu, the names joined as in earlier parts; the English spells Vucub, as in Vucub Caquix.

sentences.t: Are curi Hunhunahpu e caib xe ralcualah, e pu caib v ꜭahol: Hunbaꜩ vbi nabeal, Hunchouen chicut vbi vcabal.
sentences.l: This then Hunhunahpu, they two they-were-his-offspring, they also two his son: Hunbaꜩ its-name the-first, Hunchouen again-then its-name the-second.
sentences.i: As for Hunhunahpu, two were born to him, two sons: Hunbatz was the name of the first, and Hunchouen the name of the second.
sentences.n: e caib 'they (were) two': e, the plural, before the numeral. ralcualah: r- 'his' + alcual 'children' (al, a woman's child, + ꜭahol, a man's son, made one word, as ivalcual 'your children' in 006; toggle alk'wal) + -ah, which makes a verb: 'they were his children', i.e. he begot them. The make-up is inferred; the sense is clear. Brasseur reads e caib otherwise, 'these Hunhun-Ahpu were two', and his note says that from here the name stands for both brothers; here the two are taken as the sons (inferred). v ꜭahol 'his sons'. nabeal 'the first' (nabe 'first' + -al) and vcabal 'the second', as in 005. Hunbaꜩ and Hunchouen (MS hun baꜩ, hun chouen, joined as in earlier parts) are calendar names, hun 'one' + a day. Brasseur's note gives batz as the eleventh day of the K'iche' count, also 'thread' and 'monkey', and chouen as the eleventh day of the Maya (Yucatec) count, so the two names may be the same day in two languages (inferred). Ximénez writes the plain tz ligature, but the day and the word are the known b'atz', so the toggle shows Junb'atz', as Ꜩiz was given Tz'iis in 005; the English writes Hunbatz.

sentences.t: Are cut vbi qui chuch va Xbaquiyalo, chuꜭhaxic rixoquil Hunhunahpu.
sentences.l: This then its-name of-their-mother this Xbaquiyalo, it-is-said, his-wife of-Hunhunahpu.
sentences.i: And the name of their mother was Xbaquiyalo, as she is called, the wife of Hunhunahpu.
sentences.n: va 'this' points to the name. Xbaquiyalo: x- marks a woman's name, as in Xmucane; the rest is unclear. Brasseur cites Ximénez's 'huesos atados' ('bound bones'), from bac 'bone' + yal; the name is kept untranslated. rixoquil 'his wife': r- 'his' + ixoc 'woman' + -il.

sentences.t: Are curi Vvcub Hunahpu mahabi rixoquil, xa vlaquel.
sentences.l: This then Vvcub Hunahpu there-was-not his-wife, only vlaquel(?).
sentences.i: As for Vucub Hunahpu, he had no wife; he was alone.
sentences.n: mahabi rixoquil 'there was not his wife': K'iche' has no verb 'have', and says 'there is (not) his wife'. vlaquel occurs once in the first part, where its sense was left open. Here Brasseur renders it 'célibataire', unmarried; 'alone, single' is inferred from that and from the context. The toggle keeps 001's ulaqel.

sentences.t: Xa pu v cab xa ꜭahol vꜭoheic, e nimac ahnaoh, nim puch quetamabal, e nicvachinel varal chuvach vleuh; xa vꜩ qui ꜭoheic, qui yaqueic puch.
sentences.l: Only also its two only son its-being, they great thinkers, great also their-knowledge, they seers here on-face of-earth; only good their being, their yaqueic(?) also.
sentences.i: The two were only boys, yet they were great thinkers and great in knowledge, seers here on the face of the earth; good was their life and good their bearing.
sentences.n: MS xapu vcab, divided v cab as in the last part, where it was 'the second'; here it is read with Brasseur's u cab 'the two of them' (toggle u kab', as 008). xa ꜭahol vꜭoheic 'only boys their being' is taken as 'they were still only boys' (inferred; Brasseur 'by their nature'). e nimac ahnaoh, nim puch quetamabal is a couplet: ahnaoh 'thinker, one who knows' (ah- + naoh 'mind'), as in the first part; quetamabal 'their knowledge', qu- (qui- 'their' before a vowel) + etamabal, from etamah 'know'. The last letter of nimac is blotted; read c with Brasseur (nimak). Brasseur's OCR has alinaoh for ahnaoh. nicvachinel 'seers', as in 002 (an agent noun built on vach 'face, eye'; uncertain). yaqueic is not otherwise known; paired with ꜭoheic 'being', it is taken as 'their bearing, their ways' (Brasseur 'coutumes'), a guess.

sentences.t: Xquicutu nauiquil chi qui vach ri Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen, v ꜭahol Hunhunahpu:
sentences.l: They-showed nauiquil(?) to their face the Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen, his son Hunhunahpu:
sentences.i: Every art was shown before the eyes of Hunbatz and Hunchouen, the sons of Hunhunahpu:
sentences.n: xquicutu 'they showed': x- + qui- 'they' + cutu, the verb ꜭut 'show' of vcutunizaxic in the first part. Ximénez writes plain c (Brasseur x-qui qutu); the toggle gives k' because the word is known. Who did the showing is not said, so the English makes it passive. nauiquil is not otherwise known; Brasseur renders it 'the whole of knowledge', and 'every art' is inferred from him and from the list that follows. chi qui vach 'before their faces'. v ꜭahol 'his sons' is written above hunhunahpu with a caret; it is printed in place, as Brasseur has it.

sentences.t: e ahzu, e ahbix, e ahpub, ahꜩibenai pu, ahcot, e ahxit, e ahpuvac xe vxic ri Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen.
sentences.l: they flute-players, they singers, they blowgunners, writers also, carvers, they jewel-workers, they silver-workers they-became the Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen.
sentences.i: Hunbatz and Hunchouen became flute players and singers, blowgunners, painters and writers, carvers, jewelers and silversmiths.
sentences.n: A list of crafts, each with ah- 'one who, one of' (as in ahꜫih 'day-keeper'): zu 'flute', bix 'song', pub 'blowgun', ꜩibenai from ꜩib 'write, paint' (Brasseur: more than a plain painter or writer), cot 'carve' (Brasseur ahqot), xit 'jade, precious stone', puvac 'silver, metal'. In ahzu the z has a long tail like a cedilla (as zakhuluhuh in 006); it is read z with Brasseur. In ahpub the ah is blotted or written over; read with Brasseur. Toggle: ahꜩibenai is given ajtz'ib'enai, with the tz' of the known word 'write' (xchicaꜯibah in the first part), though Ximénez writes the plain tz ligature here (as Ꜩiz was given Tz'iis in 005). ahcot keeps the plain k of 006's coto (Brasseur's q suggests k'ot; to be decided with it). xe vxic 'they became'.

sentences.t: Are curi Hunhunahpu, Vcub Hunahpu xa zac, xa chaah chi qui bano hutaꜫih;
sentences.l: This then Hunhunahpu, Vcub Hunahpu only white(?), only ball-game they-do every-day;
sentences.i: As for Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu, every day they did nothing but play at dice and play at ball;
sentences.n: Vcub is written with one v here only, elsewhere vvcub; printed as written, with the same toggle Wuqub'. xa zac, xa chaah 'only white, only play' is a couplet. chaah is the ball game (Brasseur's note: the game of ball), the word of 005's 'his play was with the great mountains'. zac 'white' is taken with Brasseur as the white dice or knucklebones; inferred. chi qui bano 'they would do': chi + qui- 'they' + ban 'do' + -o. hutaꜫih 'every day' (hun 'one' + tac 'each' + ꜫih 'day'): the q-shaped letter is read ꜫ, where Brasseur has g (hutagih).

sentences.t: xa e cacab chi qui culelaah quib, e cahib chi conohel ta que cuchmaihic pa hom.
sentences.l: only they two-by-two(?) they-culelaah(?) themselves, they four all when they-gathered in ball-court.
sentences.i: two against two they would face each other, all four of them, when they gathered in the ball court.
sentences.n: cacab is clearly b in the manuscript (Brasseur cacap, 'every two days'); it is read here as 'two by two', a doubling of cab 'two' (inferred). qui culelaah quib: quib 'themselves, one another'; culelaah is not otherwise known and 'face each other' is a guess, perhaps from culel 'opponent'. e cahib chi conohel 'four in all': cahib 'four', conohel 'all of them'. que cuchmaihic 'they gathered' is inferred from Brasseur ('se réunissaient'). hom is the ball court: Brasseur's note gives the Nahuatl name tlachco and says the place was in truth a temple. It was a walled alley where the heavy rubber ball was struck with the hips, not the hands.

sentences.t: Chul cu ri Voc ilol que, v zamahel Huracan, chi Chipi Caculha, Raxa Caculha.
sentences.l: He-comes-here then the Voc seer of-them, his messenger of-Huracan, of Youngest Thunderbolt, Green Thunderbolt.
sentences.i: And the Voc would come to watch them, the messenger of Huracan, of Youngest Thunderbolt and Green Thunderbolt.
sentences.n: The Voc is a bird; Brasseur gives Ximénez's gloss 'gavilán', a hawk. It is kept as a name. chul 'he comes here': ch- + ul 'arrive here', as in 007 (Brasseur ch'ul). ilol que 'one who sees them': il 'see' + agent -ol, as in the first part. zamahel 'messenger': zamah 'errand, task' + agent -el. Huracan, Youngest Thunderbolt and Green Thunderbolt are the three of the Heart of Sky in the first part. The manuscript has huracan chichipicaculha: printed chi Chipi Caculha, 'of Youngest Thunderbolt'. Brasseur has no chi, and it may be a doubled syllable (chi chi-).

sentences.t: Are curi Voc mavi nah varal chuvach vleuh, mavi nah chi Xibalba; chire libahchi chopon chic chi cah ruꜭ Huracan.
sentences.l: This then Voc not far here on-face of-earth, not far at Xibalba; because quickly he-arrives again at sky with Huracan.
sentences.i: This Voc was not far from here on the face of the earth, nor far from Xibalba; for in an instant he would be back in the sky with Huracan.
sentences.n: mavi nah … mavi nah 'not far … not far': the couplet sets the earth beside Xibalba, the world below, named here for the first time; the colonial missionaries took Xibalba for 'hell' (Brasseur's note). The name is kept. chire 'because, for'. libahchi 'in an instant' is inferred from Brasseur ('en un moment'); the word is not otherwise known. chopon 'he arrives there': ch- + opon 'arrive (there)' (Brasseur ch'opon). ruꜭ 'with him'.

sentences.t: Xe yaluh varal chuvach vleuh; xcaminac ca cut qui chuch ri Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen.
sentences.l: They-stayed-long here on-face of-earth; she-had-died ca then their mother the Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen.
sentences.i: They stayed long here on the face of the earth; and the mother of Hunbatz and Hunchouen died.
sentences.n: xe yaluh 'they stayed a long time' is inferred from Brasseur ('tandis qu'ils demeuraient'; in his note on Xbaquiyalo he gives yaloh 'separate, hold back, stay'). xcaminac 'she had died': x- + caminac 'dead' (cam 'die' + -inac, the perfect). The manuscript has xcaminac cacut; Brasseur too has x-caminak ca cut (the OCR displaces it to another line); ca is left out of the English (perhaps 'then, still'). The mother is Xbaquiyalo.

sentences.t: Are cut vbeel Xibalba xe chaah vi, ta xquita cut Huncame, Vvcub Came, rahaual Xibalba.
sentences.l: This then its-road Xibalba they-played there, then they-heard-it then Huncame, Vvcub Came, its-lords Xibalba.
sentences.i: It was on the road to Xibalba that they played, and Huncame and Vucub Came, the lords of Xibalba, heard them.
sentences.n: vbeel 'its road': v- + be 'road' + -el. xe chaah vi 'they played there': chaah as a verb, with xe- 'they'; vi points back to the place. xquita 'they heard': x- + qui- + ta 'hear'. Huncame 'One Death' and Vvcub Came 'Seven Death' are calendar names like Hunhunahpu and Vvcub Hunahpu: came is cam 'die', the day Death (Brasseur). They are kept as names (MS hun came, joined as Huncame), and the English spells Vucub. rahaual Xibalba 'the lords of Xibalba': r- 'its' + ahau 'lord' + -al.

sentences.t: “Naqui pa ri caban chuvach vleuh? Xa que micnohic, xa pu que huminic.
sentences.l: “What (pa) the is-done on-face of-earth? Only they micnohic(?), only also they huminic(?).
sentences.i: “What is this that is being done on the face of the earth? They do nothing but stamp and clamour.
sentences.n: The lords speak. Naqui pa 'what is it': naqui 'what' + pa, written as one word, Naquipa, in earlier parts. caban 'is done': c- (ongoing) + ban 'do', here with a passive sense (inferred). que micnohic, que huminic: que is c- (ongoing) + e 'they'. Both verbs are not otherwise known. Brasseur's OCR is garbled at the first (quenienotic), and he renders the pair 'who make it tremble, who raise such a tumult'; 'stamp and clamour' is a guess from him and from the noise of the game.

sentences.t: Quebe ta tacoc varal tah; que vl chaah vi, que ca chac ta cut.
sentences.l: Let-them-go (ta) be-summoned here (tah); they come-here play there, them we-defeat (ta) then.
sentences.i: Let them be sent for, let them come here; let them come and play here, so that we may beat them.
sentences.n: quebe 'let them go': que 'they' + be 'go', written as one word (toggle keb'e). tacoc 'be summoned', from taq 'send, send for' (Brasseur tak-oc, his k standing for q) with -oc (taca 'send' in 007; toggle taqoq). ta and tah are the particles of wishing. que vl chaah vi 'they come here to play'. que ca chac 'we beat them': que, c- (ongoing) + e 'them', the object, + ca- 'we' + chac 'beat, win' (inferred from Brasseur's 'afin que nous les vainquions'; compare chacatahic 'being brought low'). The modern verb 'win' is ch'ak, but the word is not certain here and the toggle respells the letters.

sentences.t: Xa mahabi canimaxic cumal, mahabi qui nim, ma pu habi qui xob cuxic; xax que hiquic vloc pa ca vi,” xe ꜭha cut conoh Xibalba.
sentences.l: Only there-is-not our-being-obeyed by-them, there-is-not their respect, nor also there-is their fear of-our-being; truly they hiquic(?) hither on our heads,” they-said then all Xibalba.
sentences.i: We are not obeyed by them at all; they have no respect, they have no fear of what we are; they only brawl above our heads,” said all of Xibalba.
sentences.n: canimaxic 'our being obeyed': ca- 'our' + nim 'great' made a verb, 'honour, obey', + passive -ax- + -ic. qui nim 'their respect' (inferred), the same nim. qui xob 'their fear'. cuxic 'our being': c- (ca- 'our' before a vowel) + vxic 'being'; Brasseur k'uxic, his k standing for q, so the toggle gives quxik, as 008's qumal. hiquic is not otherwise known; 'brawl' follows Brasseur ('se batailler'), a guess. pa ca vi 'on our heads': vi 'head' (toggle wi'), as pa qui vi in 003 and 007. conoh 'all of them', short for conohel (Brasseur's note).

sentences.t: Ta xqui cam qui naoh conohel ri qui bi Huncame, Vvcub Came, e nimac catol ꜩih.
sentences.l: Then they took their thought all, the their names Huncame, Vvcub Came, they great cutters of-word.
sentences.i: Then they all took counsel, those whose names are Huncame and Vucub Came, the great judges.
sentences.n: xqui cam qui naoh 'they took their thought', took counsel: cam 'take' (toggle k'am, as in 002 and 008; Brasseur qam). catol ꜩih 'cutter of the word', a judge: catol is the agent noun of cat 'cut, decide' (006's xquicat). Brasseur has gatoltzih (his g is ꜫ), and the toggle restores q'atol. nimac 'great' (plural): Huncame and Vucub Came are the highest judges of Xibalba.

sentences.t: Are curi ahauab ronohel yaol v patan, rahauarem puch huhun chi ahauab rumal Huncame, Vvcub Came.
sentences.l: This then lords all, given(?) its-duty, his-lordship also each of lords by Huncame, Vvcub Came.
sentences.i: All the lords had their offices given them, and each of the lords his rule, by Huncame and Vucub Came.
sentences.n: ahauab 'lords': ahau 'lord' + plural -ab. yaol: ya 'give' + -ol, an agent form ('giver'), here taken as 'given' (inferred; Brasseur: the princes were tributaries of their empire). v patan 'its duty': patan is the service or tribute owed to a lord, here the office of each lord of Xibalba; the word comes back with each pair below. rahauarem 'his lordship, his rule': ahau + -arem, an abstract noun. huhun chi 'each one of'.

sentences.t: Are curi Xiquiripat, Cuchumaquic vbi ahau; are cut qui patan ri quic chu yabih vinac.
sentences.l: This then Xiquiripat, Cuchumaquic its-name lord; this then their duty the blood that-it-sickens person.
sentences.i: There were the lords named Xiquiripat and Cuchumaquic; their office was the blood, that it should make people sick.
sentences.n: The lords of Xibalba under the two come in pairs, each pair with its office, to the end of ¶13. Xiquiripat and Cuchumaquic are kept as names. Brasseur (Xiqiripat, Cuchumaquiq) renders the first 'flying basket' (hotte volante) and the second 'gathered blood' (cuchuma + quiq), and makes the pair lords over people with fluxes of blood; only quic 'blood' is clear (toggle kik', the known word; Brasseur quiq). In the names the toggle keeps the letters. chu yabih 'that it sicken': ch- + u- 'it' (the blood, taken as the subject) + yab 'sick' + -ih (inferred). vbi ahau 'the name of the lord', singular for the pair.

sentences.t: Are chi curi Ahalpuh, Ahalꜫana chic qui ahauab.
sentences.l: This again then Ahalpuh, Ahalꜫana also their lords.
sentences.i: Next were Ahalpuh and Ahalq'ana, lords also.
sentences.n: Are chi curi 'and next': chi is chic 'again, also' with its c shared with curi (toggle chik); it opens each new pair of lords. Ahal- is ah 'one who' + -al (unclear); Ahalpuh is taken as 'Maker of Pus' (puh 'pus') and Ahalꜫana as 'Maker of Yellow' (ꜫana, see the next unit), after Brasseur's 'who works the pus' and 'who works the water that runs from sores'; inferred, kept as names. The tresillo is read where Brasseur has g; the English writes Ahalq'ana, as Q'ucumatz. qui ahauab 'their lords', lords of theirs, of Xibalba.

sentences.t: Are cut cahauarem ri chi zipohic vinac, chi pe puh chirih racan, chi pe ꜫana chirih vvach, Chuꜫanal chuꜭhaxic.
sentences.l: This then their-lordship the that swells person, that comes pus behind his-legs, that comes yellow on his-face, Chuꜫanal it-is-called.
sentences.i: Their rule was this: that people should swell, that pus should come out on their legs, that yellow should come over their faces, what is called Chuq'anal.
sentences.n: cahauarem 'their lordship': c- 'their' (qui- before a vowel) + ahauarem. chi zipohic 'that he swell'. chi pe … chi pe 'that it come … that it come' is a couplet: puh 'pus' on the legs, ꜫana on the face. chirih racan 'behind his legs' (Brasseur has puh rakan, without chirih); chirih vvach 'on his face' (chi + r- + ih 'back, surface'). ꜫana is taken as ꜫan 'yellow' (008's ꜫan) + -a, and Chuꜫanal as a yellowing sickness, which Brasseur calls 'a kind of jaundice'; inferred. The first letter of ꜫana and the tresillo of Chuꜫanal were checked at 2× (Brasseur gana, Chuganal): the same letter, not a t.

sentences.t: Cate cut rahauarem Ahalpuh, Ahalꜫana vi.
sentences.l: Then then his-lordship Ahalpuh, Ahalꜫana there.
sentences.i: Such was the rule of Ahalpuh and Ahalq'ana.
sentences.n: Cate cut 'so then' closes the pair; are … vi closes the later ones. rahauarem 'his lordship', singular for the pair, as vbi ahau above. vi points back: 'in this it lay'.

sentences.t: Are chi curi ahau Chamiabac, Chamiaholom, rahchami Xibalba; xa bac qui chamiy.
sentences.l: This again then lord Chamiabac, Chamiaholom, its-staff-bearers Xibalba; only bone their staff.
sentences.i: Next were the lords Chamiabac and Chamiaholom, the staff-bearers of Xibalba; their staffs were only bone.
sentences.n: This chi is written above the line between are and curi; printed in place, as Brasseur has it. chamiy 'staff, rod', the staff an officer carries; rahchami 'its staff-bearers': r- 'its' + ah- 'one who' + chami(y). Brasseur: the officers the Spaniards called alguaciles. The names are Chamia + bac 'bone' and Chamia + holom 'head, skull', 'Bone Staff' and 'Skull Staff' (Brasseur's reading), kept as names. Here the manuscript writes Chamia- (chamia bac, chamia holom), two lines on Chamiya-; each is printed as written.

sentences.t: Are cut cahchamiyal ri chi baquir vinac, qui ꜩih chi bac, chi holom chic ta chi camic, ꜩiyah bac xu pan chi camouic.
sentences.l: This then their-staff-office the that grows-bony person, truly to bone, to skull now when he-dies, ꜩiyah(?) bone it pan(?) at taking(?).
sentences.i: Their office as staff-bearers was to waste people to the bone, truly to bone and skull, so that when they died there was only bare bone to take up.
sentences.n: cahchamiyal 'their staff-office': c- 'their' + ah-chamiy + -al. chi baquir 'that he grow bony': bac 'bone' + -ir 'become'. qui ꜩih, written apart, is taken as quiꜩih 'truly' (Brasseur quitzih), as in earlier parts (toggle qi tzij). chi bac, chi holom 'to bone, to skull', a couplet. ꜩiyah and pan are not otherwise known; Brasseur gives the end as 'so that at his death there was only a skeleton to take up', and the English follows him (guess). camouic is taken as cam 'take' + -ou- + -ic, the form of 006's xcamouic, not cam 'die' of camic just before: Brasseur prints qamouic (his q = ꜭ), 'to take up', and the toggle shows k'amowik as in 006 (inferred).

sentences.t: Are v patan vi Chamiyabac, Chamiyaholom qui bi.
sentences.l: This its duty there Chamiyabac, Chamiyaholom their name.
sentences.i: That was the office of those named Chamiyabac and Chamiyaholom.
sentences.n: MS chamiya bac chamiyaholom: the names here have Chamiya-, with the y of chamiy 'staff', where two lines up the manuscript has Chamia-. Both are printed as written (Brasseur Chamia- in both places). qui bi 'their names' after the names: 'Chamiyabac and Chamiyaholom by name'.

sentences.t: Are chi curi ahau Ahalmez, Ahaltocob qui bi.
sentences.l: This again then lord Ahalmez, Ahaltocob their name.
sentences.i: Next were the lords named Ahalmez and Ahaltocob.
sentences.n: Ahalmez 'Maker of Filth' (mez 'sweepings, rubbish') and Ahaltocob 'Maker of Misery' (tocob 'pity, misery', the word of 006's tocobah 'take pity'), after Brasseur ('qui travaille les immondices', 'qui produit la misère'); inferred, and kept as names. Brasseur prints Ahaltogob (g = ꜫ) here; Ximénez writes plain c, and the toggle restores q' as in 006/007's toq'ob'.

sentences.t: Are qui patan vi xa chi culvachih vinac, vve ꜩamez, ve pe pu chirih ha, chuva ha, chi culvachix vi, xa chi qui tocota, chi be hupul oc chuvach vleuh, ta chi camic.
sentences.l: This their duty there only that they-meet-face-to-face person, if ꜩamez(?), if comes also behind house, at-front house, that he-is-met there, only that they tocota(?) him, that he-goes face-down onto on-face of-earth, then he-dies.
sentences.i: Their office was to meet people face to face wherever they might be, behind the house or before its door: there a man would be met, and they would strike him down, and he would fall face down on the earth and die.
sentences.n: culvachih 'meet face to face': cul 'meet' + vach 'face' + -ih; then culvachix, its passive, 'he is met' (inferred; Brasseur 'faire trouver l'homme en face'). vve … ve 'whether … whether': taken as ve 'if', written vv the first time; Brasseur divides u ve (uve tzamez). Since the first v is not explained, the toggle respells the letters (uwe), as vvach gives uwach. ꜩamez is not otherwise known (Brasseur 'avec la trahison'); the English covers it with 'wherever'. chirih ha, chuva ha 'behind the house, at the front of the house' is a couplet: ha 'house' as in 004 (toggle ja), chuva 'at its front, its mouth' (inferred). tocota is not otherwise known (Brasseur togo-ta); beside the name Ahaltocob it may be 'bring to misery', and 'strike down' is a guess. hupul oc 'face down into': hupul as 007's hupulic, oc the ending of direction. Brasseur here has 'tomber la bouche en l'air', mouth upward, against the 'face down' of 007 and 008; the English keeps those parts' reading (inferred).

sentences.t: Are cut cahauarem Ahalmez, Ahaltocob, que vꜭhaxic.
sentences.l: This then their-lordship Ahalmez, Ahaltocob, as they-are-called.
sentences.i: That was the rule of Ahalmez and Ahaltocob, as they are called.
sentences.n: que vꜭhaxic 'as they are called' closes this pair, as chuꜭhaxic closed the second.

sentences.t: Are chi curi ahau Xic, Patan qui bi.
sentences.l: This again then lord Xic, Patan their name.
sentences.i: Next were the lords named Xic and Patan.
sentences.n: Brasseur takes Xic as 'hawk' (épervier) and Patan as a basket for carrying loads (hotte), from which, he says, come 'office, charge and tribute', often the same word: patan is the 'duty, office' of every pair of lords here, a duty being a load carried. Both are kept as names, and the toggle keeps the letters.

sentences.t: Are cahauarem ri vinac chi cam pa be, xa rax camic chuꜭhaxic: chi pe quic pa chi, ta chi camic chu xavah quic.
sentences.l: This their-lordship the person that dies on road, only green death it-is-called: that comes blood in mouth, then he-dies he-vomits blood.
sentences.i: Their rule was over people who die on the road, sudden death, as it is called: blood comes into the mouth, and they die vomiting blood.
sentences.n: rax camic 'green death': rax 'green, raw, fresh' also means 'sudden', and Brasseur has 'mort subite'. pa chi 'in the mouth' (chi 'mouth', toggle chi'): the manuscript has pa | chi across the line, where Brasseur has pu chi; the image is followed. chu xavah quic 'he vomits blood': ch- + u- + xavah 'vomit'. quic 'blood' (toggle kik').

sentences.t: Xa huhun chi patan qui telelaon, xa chi qui cozih vculel vꜭux vinac ta chi cam pa be, xa chi qui culmah apon oc ve chibinic chi cul.
sentences.l: Only each of burden they telelaon(?), only that they squeeze(?) his-throat(?) his-heart person so-that he-dies on road, only that they culmah(?) arriving (oc) if he-walks at throat(?).
sentences.i: Each of them bore his load of office: they would seize a man by the throat and the heart, so that he died on the road; they would bring it on him as he walked, at the throat.
sentences.n: The least certain sentence of the part. huhun chi patan 'each a load': patan as the carried load (see Patan). telelaon is not otherwise known; taken with tel 'carry on the shoulder' (a guess; compare qui telen in 005). cozih 'squeeze' is inferred from Brasseur ('étreindre'; he prints gozih, his g for ꜫ, and the toggle respells Ximénez's c). vculel: Brasseur's OCR has u cue!, his French 'the throat'; perhaps v- 'his' + cul 'neck' (008's vcul) + -el, inferred, and the toggle respells the letters. vꜭux 'his heart': the manuscript has a q-shaped letter (vqux; Brasseur's OCR u gux), printed vꜭux as the known word of Vꜭux Cah; by the letter alone it could be ꜭ or ꜫ. culmah and the closing chi cul are left as Brasseur reads them ('bringing it on him suddenly at the throat, as he walked'), and the English follows him (guess). chibinic 'he walks': ch- + bin 'walk' + -ic.

sentences.t: Are cut cahauarem Xic, Patan vi.
sentences.l: This then their-lordship Xic, Patan there.
sentences.i: That was the rule of Xic and Patan.
sentences.n: The list of the lords of Xibalba ends here: Huncame and Vvcub Came at the head, and five pairs under them, each named with its office.

sentences.t: Are cut xqui cuc qui naoh ri ta xe ꜩaixic, ta xe cotobax puch Hunhunahpu, Vvcub Hunahpu.
sentences.l: This then they-cuc(?) their thought the that they-be-ꜩai(?), that they-be-cotob(?) also Hunhunahpu, Vvcub Hunahpu.
sentences.i: Then they gathered their counsel, so that Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu might be hunted down and punished.
sentences.n: xqui cuc qui naoh 'they gathered their thought' is read with Brasseur (c'uq, 'se réunirent en conseil'); this cuc is not the cuc 'quetzal feathers' of the first part, and the toggle keeps the letters (kuk). The first part has the same gathering of thought with another verb, xqui cuch qui ꜩih, qui naoh 'they joined their word, their thought'; cuc may be a form of that cuch (inferred). ta xe ꜩaixic, ta xe cotobax puch is a couplet of passives with xe- 'they'. ꜩaixic 'be pursued' and cotobax 'be punished' follow Brasseur ('poursuivre et châtier'); both are inferred, cotobax has the letters of 006's vcotobahic, read there as 'its digging'; whether they are one verb is not known.

sentences.t: Are xqui raih Xibalba ri queꜩabal Hunhunahpu, Vvcub Hunahpu, ri qui ꜩuun, qui bate, qui pachcab, qui yachvach, vachzot puch, qui cauubal Hunhunahpu, Vvcub Hunahpu.
sentences.l: This they-wanted Xibalba the their-play-gear Hunhunahpu, Vvcub Hunahpu, the their leather(?), their ring(?), their hand-guard(?), their yachvach(?), face-piece(?) also, their finery Hunhunahpu, Vvcub Hunahpu.
sentences.i: What Xibalba wanted was the gaming gear of Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu: their leathers, their rings, their hand-guards, their headdresses and face-pieces, the finery of Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu.
sentences.n: xqui raih 'they wanted' (008's raih, inferred; Brasseur here 'désiraient'). Brasseur's French has the lords wanting 'to hold up to scorn' (livrer au mépris) the brothers and their gear; the reading of queꜩabal as 'gear for play' is inferred. queꜩabal 'their gear for play': qu- (qui- before a vowel) + eꜩ 'play' + -abal, the noun of means; the toggle gives tz', the modern word for play (etz'anem), though Ximénez writes the plain ligature. The list names a ball player's gear, after Brasseur ('leurs boucliers de cuir, leurs anneaux, leurs gants, leurs couronnes avec les casques'): ꜩuun is taken as leather or hide (perhaps the modern tz'um 'skin'; the toggle respells the letters), bate as a ring (Brasseur 'anneaux'; guess), pachcab as a guard for the hand (cab 'hand'; Brasseur pachgab, toggle q'ab' as 008's vcab), yachvach and vachzot as headgear or face-pieces (vach 'face'; guess). In qui yachvach (MS qui yach|vach) the y is faint; read with Brasseur. cauubal 'finery', as 006's caubal 'my beauty'.

sentences.t: Are chicut xchi ca biyh chic qui biye chi Xibalba.
sentences.l: This again-then shall we tell also their going to Xibalba.
sentences.i: And now we shall tell of their going to Xibalba.
sentences.n: The words of the part's opening come back with a new subject. qui biye 'their going' (perhaps be 'go', or bin 'walk'; Brasseur 'leur voyage'), inferred. The manuscript has qui byc with a mark over the y, and the last letter is an open c or e; printed biye with Brasseur, a doubtful reading.

sentences.t: Xe canah cu canoc ri Hunbaꜩ, Chouen, v ꜭahol Hunhunahpu.
sentences.l: They-stayed then remaining the Hunbaꜩ, Chouen, his son Hunhunahpu.
sentences.i: Hunbatz and Chouen, the sons of Hunhunahpu, were left behind.
sentences.n: xe canah 'they stayed', and canoc 'left behind', the same root canah 'remain' with -oc: said twice for weight. The manuscript, like Brasseur, has Chouen here without Hun; it is printed and translated as written (Brasseur: Chouen for Hunchouen).

sentences.t: Xcaminac oc qui chuch; ca chuvi chic qui chacatahic chic Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen cumal Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: She-had-died already their mother; ca on-top again their being-brought-low again Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen by Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: Their mother had already died. And later comes the downfall of Hunbatz and Hunchouen, at the hands of Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
sentences.n: xcaminac oc 'she had already died': oc 'still, already'. ca chuvi chic 'later, further on' is inferred (chuvi 'on top of, after'; Brasseur 'ensuite de cela'); the narrator points ahead, as at the end of the last part. qui chacatahic 'their being brought low', the word used for Vucub Caquix and his sons: Hunbaꜩ and Hunchouen too will be humbled, by Hunahpu and Xbalanque. The part ends here, where Brasseur ends the first chapter of his second part.
